c-fm-01-q046.trap: Bed rest slows recovery compared to remaining active, and imaging (CT/MRI) is unnecessary within the first 4-6 weeks in the absence of progressive neurologic deficits or red flags.

A.clue: Prolonged immobilization in bed
A.fit: Not here: bed rest delays recovery and worsens back pain disability
A.tempting: intuitively rests injured lumbar muscles and relieves radicular pain

B.clue: Computed tomographic imaging of lumbar spine
B.fit: Not here: normal neurologic exam, no red flags, duration < 4 weeks
B.tempting: evaluates herniated disc causing radiating pain down left leg

C.fit: Not here: reserved for radiculopathy failing conservative therapy > 6 weeks
C.tempting: rapidly reduces nerve root inflammation in radiating pain

D.clue: Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic
D.fit: Here: 1-week back pain radiating to leg, normal neurologic exam

E.fit: Not here: systemic steroids lack proven efficacy for acute mechanical back pain
E.tempting: potent anti-inflammatory for acute radiating sciatica

algorithm.title: Acute mechanical low back pain and sciatica

nodes.text: Acute low back pain with or without radiculopathy: screen for red flags (cauda equina, fever, trauma, progressive weakness)
**Red flags absent + duration < 4 to 6 weeks:** no imaging indicated; initiate conservative medical management
First-line pharmacotherapy: oral NSAIDs (ibuprofen or naproxen) or acetaminophen
Advise continuing light daily activities and early mobilization; avoid prolonged bed rest
**Radicular symptoms or severe pain refractory after 4 to 6 weeks:** obtain noncontrast lumbar spine MRI
Physical therapy and core stabilization exercises once acute severe pain improves

triggers.text: 1-week history of low back pain that radiates to the left buttock
diffuse tenderness over the paraspinal muscles of the lumbosacral area
no tenderness over the spine
sensory examination shows no abnormalities

c-fm-01-q047.boardCall: Major depressive symptoms (anhedonia, guilt, insomnia, impaired concentration) -> Screen directly for suicidal ideation
c-fm-01-q047.hinge: Multiple SIGECAPS criteria for major depression with excessive maternal guilt and hopelessness require immediate, direct screening for suicidal ideation.
c-fm-01-q047.trap: Normalizing her distress as ordinary parenting stress minimizes potentially life-threatening depression.

A.clue: Dismissive normalization of clinical depression
A.fit: Not here: dismisses core symptoms of clinical depression and guilt
A.tempting: reassuring colloquial empathy for parenting challenges

B.fit: Not here: ignores root major depression and potential suicide risk
B.tempting: addresses insomnia and secondary irritability directly

C.clue: Direct, empathetic assessment of suicide risk
C.fit: Here: anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration, excessive guilt

D.clue: Premature anxiolytic pharmacotherapy
D.fit: Not here: fails to address primary depression and assess suicide risk
D.tempting: targets perceived anxiety and stress coping

E.fit: Not here: minor alcohol use is secondary, depression is primary
E.tempting: alcohol can worsen mood stability and sleep quality

algorithm.title: Depression screening and suicide risk assessment

nodes.text: Depressive symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, guilt, poor concentration): evaluate for major depressive disorder (SIGECAPS)
Screen directly and nonjudgmentally for suicidal ideation, intent, plan, and access to lethal means
**Active suicidal ideation with intent or plan:** immediate psychiatric evaluation + emergency safety hold
**Passive ideation without intent or plan:** safety planning + lethal means restriction + close outpatient follow-up
First-line depression treatment: cognitive behavioral therapy and/or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Screen for substance use, bipolar disorder, and underlying medical etiologies (TSH, vitamin B12)

triggers.text: I am so irritable with my boys, and they are good kids.
difficulty concentrating during the day and falling asleep at night
no longer is interested in activities that she used to enjoy

c-fm-01-q048.boardCall: Obese smoker with stage 1 hypertension + largest blood pressure reduction -> Weight loss of 9 kg (20 lb)
c-fm-01-q048.hinge: Weight loss reduces systolic blood pressure by approximately 1 mm Hg per 1 kg lost (5-10 mm Hg for 9-10 kg), making it the single most potent non-pharmacologic BP-lowering lifestyle intervention.
c-fm-01-q048.trap: Smoking cessation has immense cardiovascular mortality benefits but produces little direct long-term reduction in baseline resting blood pressure compared to significant weight loss.

A.clue: Alcohol moderation or cessation
A.fit: Not here: reduces BP by 2 to 4 mm Hg, less than 9 kg weight loss
A.tempting: known non-pharmacologic lifestyle modification for hypertension

B.fit: Not here: caffeine causes transient acute elevation but no chronic HTN
B.tempting: caffeine acutely raises blood pressure and pulse

C.fit: Not here: vital for cardiovascular survival, but minimal effect on resting BP
C.tempting: most important overall cardiovascular risk reduction strategy

D.clue: Adiposity reduction lowering peripheral resistance and sympathetic tone
D.fit: Here: BMI 33 kg/m², blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg

E.fit: Not here: minimal, transient, and inconsistent blood pressure lowering
E.tempting: non-invasive behavioral technique for autonomic regulation

F.fit: Not here: vitamin E has no proven antihypertensive efficacy
F.tempting: antioxidant marketed for vascular and cardiovascular health

nodes.text: Stage 1 hypertension (130-139 / 80-89 mm Hg) or stage 2 (>= 140/90 mm Hg): initiate comprehensive lifestyle modifications
Weight reduction in overweight/obese patients: provides largest BP reduction (~1 mm Hg per kg lost)
DASH diet (rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy): reduces systolic BP by ~11 mm Hg
Dietary sodium restriction (< 1500 mg/day optimal): reduces systolic BP by ~5-6 mm Hg
Aerobic exercise (90 to 150 minutes/week) + moderate alcohol intake (<= 1-2 drinks/day)
**Blood pressure >= 140/90 mm Hg or 10-year ASCVD risk >= 10%:** initiate first-line antihypertensive medication

triggers.text: moderately obese for 20 years and follows a high-calorie, high-fat diet
BMI is 33 kg/m²
blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg

c-fm-01-q049.boardCall: 20-year GERD history + new dysphagia/food impaction -> Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy)
c-fm-01-q049.hinge: Dysphagia (food sticking) in a patient over 50 with long-standing chronic GERD is an alarm symptom requiring upper endoscopy to rule out esophageal adenocarcinoma, stricture, or Barrett esophagus.
c-fm-01-q049.trap: Barium swallow evaluates motility or Zenker diverticulum, but upper endoscopy directly visualizes the mucosa and allows tissue biopsy of suspected malignancy.

A.clue: Fluoroscopic contrast luminal transit examination
A.fit: Not here: cannot biopsy mucosal lesions or Barrett esophagus
A.tempting: evaluates location of mechanical obstruction or food sticking

B.fit: Not here: cannot detect intraluminal mucosal malignancy or stricture
B.tempting: evaluates middle to lower chest pain and structural masses

C.fit: Not here: mechanical obstruction and malignancy must be excluded first
C.tempting: investigates intermittent food sticking and chest pain

D.clue: Direct endoscopic mucosal visualization and biopsy
D.fit: Here: 57-year-old, 20-year GERD, food sticking in chest

E.clue: Continuous wireless or catheter acid exposure recording
E.fit: Not here: patient has alarm dysphagia requiring anatomic evaluation
E.tempting: evaluates refractory GERD symptoms despite PPI therapy

nodes.text: Difficulty swallowing or food impaction in patient with chronic GERD: identify as alarm symptom
First-line diagnostic procedure: urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsies
**Esophageal adenocarcinoma or high-grade dysplasia:** staging CT/EUS + oncologic multidisciplinary management
**Peptic stricture or Schatzki ring:** endoscopic balloon dilation + high-dose daily PPI
**Eosinophilic esophagitis (trachealized rings, furrows):** swallowed topical fluticasone or budesonide
**Endoscopy unrevealing (normal mucosa):** obtain barium swallow followed by high-resolution esophageal manometry
Lifestyle modifications: elevate head of bed, avoid eating within 3 hours of sleep, and lose weight

triggers.text: 3-month history of intermittent chest pain with eating
sensation that food is stuck in his middle to lower chest
20-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with a proton pump inhibitor
relieved after he drinks a large amount of water

c-fm-01-q050.boardCall: Health education program on diet -> Measure change in participant knowledge and dietary habits
c-fm-01-q050.hinge: The effectiveness of an educational intervention is directly measured by its proximal learning and behavioral objectives (knowledge acquisition and dietary changes), rather than distant clinical endpoints in a small cohort.
c-fm-01-q050.trap: Morbidity and mortality from ischemic heart disease require large populations (thousands) and years of follow-up, which is impossible to detect in a 100-patient educational program.

A.clue: Global self-reported health survey
A.fit: Not here: confounded by comorbid conditions unrelated to diet
A.tempting: measures overall participant wellbeing after program

B.fit: Not here: measures adherence and engagement, not learning or efficacy
B.tempting: measures adherence and attendance to educational sessions

C.fit: Not here: sample size of 100 is vastly underpowered for mortality
C.tempting: definitive clinical goal of high-fiber low-cholesterol diet

D.clue: Direct assessment of educational and behavioral goals
D.fit: Here: 100-patient educational program on fiber and cholesterol

E.clue: Clinical disease incidence and event rates
E.fit: Not here: requires years of follow-up and thousands of subjects
E.tempting: evaluates actual disease reduction resulting from dietary change

nodes.text: Design health education intervention: define specific, measurable learning and behavioral goals
Measure proximal outcomes: assess pre- and post-intervention participant knowledge and dietary habits
**Knowledge improved but habits unchanged:** address behavioral barriers, self-efficacy, and environmental access
**Both knowledge and habits improved:** demonstrate educational program efficacy
Process evaluation: monitor attendance rates, participant satisfaction, and curriculum fidelity
Distant clinical endpoints (cardiovascular events, mortality): reserve for large, long-term randomized clinical trials

triggers.text: One hundred patients participate in a health education program
designed to teach health benefits of a high-fiber, low-cholesterol diet
effectiveness of this program

acute-rhinosinusitis.name: Acute rhinosinusitis
acute-rhinosinusitis.scope: Common cold, viral rhinosinusitis, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis criteria, symptomatic therapy, antibiotic stewardship
acute-rhinosinusitis.core: Acute nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and facial pressure usually reflect a self-limited viral infection; duration and course identify likely bacterial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Respiratory exposure, daycare contacts, impaired drainage from allergic inflammation
Immunocompromise, recent antibiotics, or hospitalization increases resistant-organism risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, reduced smell, maxillary tenderness; colored mucus alone does not establish bacterial infection
★ Orbital swelling, painful eye movement, reduced vision, severe headache → **complicated infection**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral mucosal edema blocks sinus drainage; secondary infection commonly pneumococcus, H influenzae, or Moraxella

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; uncomplicated illness needs neither sinus radiographs nor CT
Persistent, severe, or biphasic course identifies bacterial cases; fever alone is insufficient
Suspected orbital/intracranial extension → contrast CT; MRI for intracranial definition
Refractory or unusual infection → ENT evaluation; routine nasal swab cultures unhelpful

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Viral illness → **saline irrigation, acetaminophen/NSAID**; no antibiotics
Intranasal fluticasone for associated allergic inflammation; topical oxymetazoline at most 3 days
★ Uncomplicated bacterial illness + reliable follow-up → **watchful waiting** or antibiotics
Antibiotic choice: amoxicillin-clavulanate, usually 5–7 days in adults; penicillin allergy → doxycycline
Complication → admission, IV ampicillin-sulbactam, urgent ENT/ophthalmology; avoid empiric azithromycin because resistance

rows.label: Complications
items: Orbital cellulitis or abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess
Unnecessary antibiotics → diarrhea, C difficile, resistance

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, smoking avoidance, control allergic rhinitis
Sterile/distilled or previously boiled water for nasal irrigation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Allergic rhinitis: itching, sneezing, watery discharge without fever
Migraine: episodic disabling headache, photophobia, nausea
Dental infection: focal tooth pain, unilateral maxillary symptoms

table.title: Bacterial patterns
rows: Initial improvement → new fever or worsening symptoms

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.name: Adolescent confidentiality and care
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.scope: Confidentiality principles, exceptions to parental notification, parental requests for drug testing, encouraging family involvement
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.core: Provide adolescents private, developmentally appropriate care; explain confidentiality and its safety limits before sensitive questions.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality supports honest disclosure; consent authority and parental access vary by jurisdiction
Assent: involve the adolescent even when guardian permission remains necessary

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Interview alone** for sexual health, substance use, mood, violence, and safety
★ Explain permitted confidential services; protect portals, billing, and result notifications
Encourage trusted-adult involvement; never require disclosure for legally confidential services

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ Parental request for **drug testing** → discuss concern, interview teen; avoid covert testing
Do not promise absolute secrecy or automatically send sensitive findings to parents

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Imminent danger, suspected **abuse/neglect/exploitation** → protective disclosure and reporting
Emergency treatment when delay risks serious harm; involve guardians when feasible
Emancipated minors generally self-consent; pregnancy alone does not universally confer emancipation

rows.label: Traps
items: Minor consent rules differ for STI, contraception, pregnancy, mental health, and substance treatment
Mandatory reporting thresholds for consensual sexual activity depend on ages and local law
Disclose minimum necessary information; explain safety-driven disclosure to adolescent whenever feasible

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.evidence: Not checked online; established ethics principles; jurisdiction-specific consent/reporting law must be verified locally.

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all adults 19–59; ≥60 with risk or requesting protection
Liver disease → HepA/HepB; COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal before routine age
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Review records, contraindications, immunity; HBV serology useful, but **do not delay vaccination**
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Avoid live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza** during pregnancy or severe immunosuppression
PCV15 → PPSV23: minimum 8 weeks if immunocompromised; mild illness/antibiotics need no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern, explain benefit, recommend clearly; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

alcohol-use-disorder.name: Alcohol use disorder
alcohol-use-disorder.scope: Unhealthy alcohol use, CAGE and AUDIT screening, transaminitis (AST > ALT), motivational interviewing, naltrexone, acamprosate
alcohol-use-disorder.core: Compulsive alcohol use despite harm, impaired control, or physiologic dependence calls for nonjudgmental assessment and relapse-prevention treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, early initiation, trauma, depression, anxiety, social stress
Binge drinking and escalating tolerance; coexisting sedative use increases overdose risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Craving, failed attempts to cut down, role impairment, continued use despite consequences
AST:ALT >2, macrocytosis, elevated GGT support exposure but neither prove nor exclude disorder
★ Tremor, tachycardia, hallucinations, seizures after reduction → **withdrawal**, potentially fatal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic GABA enhancement/NMDA inhibition → compensatory adaptation; cessation unmasks CNS excitation
Mesolimbic reinforcement and stress circuitry sustain compulsive use and relapse

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screen adults using **AUDIT-C** or single-question heavy-use screen; positive result → fuller assessment
DSM-5: ≥2 of 11 criteria within 12 months; 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, ≥6 severe
CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; ≥2 positive suggests problem use, misses early risky drinking
Assess suicidality, other drugs, liver disease, nutritional deficiency, pregnancy, withdrawal history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Motivational interviewing**: elicit goals, reflect ambivalence, agree achievable change; CBT and mutual support
Withdrawal → benzodiazepines; inpatient detoxification for severe history, unstable comorbidity, or unreliable support
Thiamine promptly for malnutrition/Wernicke risk; never delay emergency glucose for hypoglycemia
Disulfiram: selected supervised abstinence; avoid severe liver/cardiac disease; alcohol exposure causes aversive reaction

rows.label: Complications
items: Cirrhosis, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, cancer, injuries, fetal alcohol effects
Wernicke encephalopathy → Korsakoff amnesia; depression and suicide risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Ongoing **relapse planning**, frequent follow-up, social support; abstinence for pregnancy or advanced liver disease
Assess hepatitis vaccination, nutrition, driving safety, medication interactions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sedative withdrawal: similar autonomic excitation with benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction
Hyperthyroidism: tremor/tachycardia without alcohol-linked time course

table.title: Relapse prevention
rows: Current opioids; acute hepatitis/severe hepatic failure

alcohol-use-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established screening and addiction-treatment principles.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Atopy, family history, allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ **No SABA-only treatment or LABA monotherapy**; current GINA differs from older intermittent-asthma teaching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings

benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.scope: Lower urinary tract symptoms, medical therapy, urinary retention and obstructive uropathy
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.core: Aging man with hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, and nocturia from benign periurethral prostatic enlargement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, androgen exposure, family history, obesity/metabolic syndrome
Anticholinergics, opioids, and sympathomimetic decongestants can precipitate retention

rows.label: Clues
items: Storage symptoms: urgency, frequency; voiding symptoms: straining, intermittency, terminal dribbling
Smooth, symmetric enlarged prostate; size correlates imperfectly with symptom severity
★ **Painful inability to void** with palpable bladder → acute urinary retention
Renal dysfunction or bilateral hydronephrosis suggests high-pressure obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dihydrotestosterone-driven transition-zone hyperplasia + alpha-adrenergic smooth-muscle tone obstruct bladder outlet

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**, symptom score, examination; review medications and neurologic disease
Postvoid residual if incomplete emptying suspected; creatinine/renal ultrasound for obstruction or renal impairment
PSA after shared decision-making if result changes management; elevation not specific for cancer

rows.label: Tx
items: Mild, nonbothersome → observation; reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol; timed voiding
★ Acute retention → **urethral catheter**, then alpha-blocker and voiding trial; suprapubic drainage if catheterization fails
★ Refractory symptoms, retention, recurrent UTIs, stones, renal impairment → **TURP or other outlet procedure**
Monitor urine output/electrolytes after relief of prolonged obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Overflow incontinence, recurrent infection, bladder stones, postrenal AKI
Postobstructive diuresis; surgery → bleeding, retrograde ejaculation, urethral stricture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid precipitating drugs; reassess progressive symptoms and residual volume
BPH does not transform into prostate cancer; continue independent cancer-risk discussion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Prostate cancer: hard asymmetric nodule
Prostatitis: tender prostate, fever; neurogenic bladder: neurologic disease, altered bladder sensation

table.title: Medication selection
rows: Large gland; reduce progression over months

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax**, contralateral weakness/numbness, or aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.scope: Median nerve entrapment, pregnancy and endocrine risk factors, Phalen and Tinel tests, wrist splinting, corticosteroid injection, surgical release
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.core: Median nerve compression at the wrist causes nocturnal paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/fluid retention, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis
Forceful repetitive hand activity, wrist trauma; dialysis-associated amyloid in selected patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Shaking hand relieves symptoms; driving or sustained wrist flexion aggravates symptoms
★ **Thenar weakness/atrophy**, dropping objects, impaired thumb opposition → advanced nerve injury
Central palm sensation usually spared because palmar cutaneous branch bypasses tunnel
Bilateral symptoms common; isolated little-finger symptoms argue against median neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Raised pressure beneath transverse carpal ligament → median nerve ischemia/demyelination
Long-standing compression progresses to axonal loss and persistent motor impairment

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical history + **Phalen/Tinel or carpal compression** findings support clinical diagnosis
Phalen: sustained wrist flexion; Tinel: percussion over median nerve reproduces distal paresthesia
★ **Nerve-conduction studies/EMG** for atypical presentation, severity assessment, or uncertain diagnosis before surgery
Targeted TSH/glucose testing when systemic disease suspected; routine wrist imaging unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild/moderate → **neutral-position wrist splint at night**, ergonomic modification
Local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms or short-term relief; pregnancy often resolves postpartum
★ Severe deficit, denervation, or failed conservative care → **surgical carpal tunnel release**
NSAIDs do not relieve the underlying compression; avoid repeated ineffective analgesic-only management

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent sensory loss and thenar wasting if severe compression persists
Injection → transient hyperglycemia, rare nerve injury; surgery → scar pain or incomplete release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce prolonged wrist flexion/extension and forceful vibration; adjust workstation and tools
Manage contributing endocrine/inflammatory disease; reassess worsening motor function promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain, dermatomal weakness/reflex changes
Ulnar neuropathy: little finger/ulnar ring symptoms, interosseous weakness
Pronator syndrome: proximal forearm pain with palmar sensory involvement

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

constipation-and-fecal-impaction.name: Constipation and fecal impaction
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.scope: Functional constipation, medication-induced constipation, fecal impaction and overflow incontinence, digital disimpaction, laxatives, fiber
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.core: Difficult, infrequent, or incomplete defecation; loose stool can represent overflow around an impacted rectal stool mass.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low fiber, immobility, dehydration, withholding, older age; childhood onset often follows painful defecation/toilet training
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, verapamil; hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Hard/lumpy stool, straining, incomplete emptying, <3 spontaneous stools/week; frequency alone insufficient
★ **Rectal fullness, paradoxical diarrhea, fecal soiling, urinary retention** → consider impaction
★ **Bleeding, anemia, weight loss, new persistent change**, severe distension/vomiting → structural evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Slow transit increases water absorption; pelvic-floor dyssynergia prevents coordinated expulsion
Stool retention stretches rectum → reduced sensation and leakage of liquid around retained mass

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ History, drug review, abdominal examination, **digital rectal examination** for stool, masses, pelvic-floor dysfunction
No alarm findings → clinical diagnosis; targeted TSH/calcium if suspected; colonoscopy for alarms or overdue screening
Refractory despite laxatives → anorectal manometry + balloon-expulsion test; then transit studies if needed
Empty rectum does not exclude proximal impaction; obstruction concern → abdominal imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Palpable hard rectal mass → **manual disimpaction**, then enemas; proximal stool → PEG after obstruction excluded
★ Uncomplicated constipation → **fiber gradually + polyethylene glycol**; hydration if depleted, scheduled postmeal toileting
Dyssynergic defecation → pelvic-floor biofeedback; stool softener alone will not correct outlet dysfunction
Opioid-induced: stimulant + osmotic laxative; refractory → naloxegol/naldemedine after excluding bowel obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Anal fissures, hemorrhoids, prolapse, stercoral ulceration/perforation, recurrent impaction
Magnesium laxatives → hypermagnesemia in CKD; phosphate enemas → electrolyte injury, especially renal disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintenance bowel regimen after disimpaction; regular activity, adequate dietary fiber, minimize constipating drugs
Avoid bulk fiber during unresolved impaction; pediatric withholding → reward-based routine, no punishment

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS-C: recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation/stool changes
Bowel obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, dilated bowel
Hirschsprung: neonatal delayed meconium, distension, absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex

table.title: Escalating agents
rows: Limited efficacy; avoid relying on it
