dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

dermatophyte-infections.name: Dermatophyte infections
dermatophyte-infections.scope: Tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, onychomycosis, potassium hydroxide preparation, oral and topical antifungals
dermatophyte-infections.core: Keratin-invading fungi cause scaly skin lesions or infected hair/nails; the anatomic site determines topical versus systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Warm humid conditions, occlusive footwear, shared showers, wrestling, infected animals or contacts
Diabetes, immunosuppression; childhood favors scalp infection; nail disease increases with age

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus and peripheral scaling; steroid exposure may distort borders and suppress inflammation
★ **Boggy tender scalp plaque** → kerion; inflammatory disease risks permanent scarring alopecia
Interdigital maceration/fissures can become bacterial entry sites

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton digest keratin in stratum corneum, hair, and nails
Follicular/deep involvement prevents topical agents from reaching the infected reservoir

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **KOH preparation of active edge** → branching septate hyphae; obtain before systemic treatment when uncertain
Scalp: hair/plucked scale microscopy and culture; nail: clipping KOH, PAS, or fungal culture
Wood lamp detects only selected organisms; negative fluorescence does not exclude tinea
Refractory/widespread infection → reassess diagnosis, adherence, resistance; fungal culture can guide further care

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Limited skin disease → **topical terbinafine** or clotrimazole; continue beyond clinical clearing
★ Hair infection → **oral griseofulvin or terbinafine**; adjunct selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread
Nail infection → confirm fungus, then oral terbinafine; baseline liver assessment; counsel slow regrowth
Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy or steroid-antifungal combinations; extensive disease may require oral antifungal

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary cellulitis, persistent nail dystrophy, recurrent infection from untreated reservoirs
Oral antifungals: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions; griseofulvin contraindicated during pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Keep feet dry**, change socks, avoid shared towels/combs, disinfect sports gear
Treat symptomatic contacts/pets and coexisting foot disease; avoid barefoot communal-shower exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Candida intertrigo: satellite pustules, scrotal involvement
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated plaques, nail pitting; alopecia areata: smooth nonscaly patches

table.title: Site clues
rows: Broken hairs, black dots, patchy alopecia
Annular plaque, advancing border, central clearing
Thick yellow brittle nail, subungual debris

dermatophyte-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatophyte diagnosis and site-based treatment.

diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or selected TCAs alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Radiculopathy: dermatomal unilateral pain with root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Burning/numb feet, reduced vibration and ankle reflexes
Orthostasis, tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, hypoglycemia unawareness
Acute isolated nerve deficit; often reversible

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia
dyslipidemia.scope: Lipid screening guidelines, ASCVD risk calculation, statin therapy indications, monitoring response to diet and pharmacotherapy
dyslipidemia.core: Excess atherogenic lipoproteins drive ASCVD; treatment intensity follows established disease, severe LDL elevation, diabetes, and estimated absolute cardiovascular risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Familial disorders, saturated-fat intake, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis
Premature ASCVD family history, CKD, smoking, inflammatory disease increase treatment benefit

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; tendon xanthomas/early corneal arcus suggest familial hypercholesterolemia
Severe triglyceride elevation: eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis; low HDL alone is not a drug target

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retained apoB-containing particles → arterial inflammation and plaque formation
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Lipid panel from age 19, at least every 5 years**; earlier/more often with risk
Nonfasting panel acceptable; markedly high triglycerides → fasting repeat/secondary-cause evaluation; Lp(a) once/lifetime
★ **PREVENT-ASCVD**, ages 30–79, LDL 70–189 without ASCVD: replaces pooled-cohort equations in 2026 guidance
Uncertain statin decision → coronary calcium; zero insufficient for deferral with diabetes, smoking, strong premature history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinical ASCVD or **LDL ≥190 mg/dL → high-intensity statin**, no risk calculation required
★ Diabetes age 40–75 → **at least moderate-intensity statin**; multiple risk factors favor high intensity
Above LDL target despite maximal statin → ezetimibe; consider PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid
Severe triglycerides ≥500 → address causes, diet, consider fenofibrate/prescription omega-3 to reduce pancreatitis risk

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; statins → myalgias, rare rhabdomyolysis, small diabetes-risk increase
Baseline ALT; CK only with symptoms/risk; most lipid-lowering drugs deferred during conception/pregnancy/lactation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mediterranean-style diet, replace saturated fats, exercise, weight reduction, smoking cessation
★ Recheck lipids **4–12 weeks after starting/changing drugs**, then every 6–12 months; assess adherence
High intensity lowers LDL ≥50%: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH; correct before labeling primary dyslipidemia
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia; treat renal cause

table.title: Risk-based primary prevention and secondary target

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ Hematemesis/melena, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia → **alarm evaluation**
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation; early satiety with recurrent vomiting → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years → upper endoscopy**; younger high-risk/alarm presentations assessed individually
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute either crystal flare → **NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; intraarticular steroid only after infection excluded
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Continue urate lowering during flares; may start during treated flare; no routine asymptomatic-hyperuricemia treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring
Weight reduction, limit alcohol/fructose; replace thiazide with losartan when feasible; retain indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles, dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Start beta-blocker only when compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires 36-hour washout
MRA requires eGFR >30, K <5; persistent EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

herpes-zoster.name: Herpes zoster
herpes-zoster.scope: Varicella zoster reactivation, dermatomal rash, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, oral antivirals, postherpetic neuralgia, Shingrix vaccine
herpes-zoster.core: Latent varicella-zoster reactivation causes painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles; ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease changes urgency and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, HIV, malignancy, transplantation, immunosuppressive drugs
Previous chickenpox or live varicella vaccination establishes latency; no new exposure required

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning/allodynia can precede eruption by days; crops crust over approximately 7–10 days
★ **V1 distribution, nasal-tip lesions, eye pain** → urgent ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus
★ **Ear vesicles + ipsilateral facial paralysis** ± hearing/vestibular symptoms → Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Multiple noncontiguous dermatomes or >20 lesions outside primary/adjacent dermatomes suggests dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced VZV-specific cellular immunity permits virus to travel from sensory ganglion to skin
Neuronal inflammation/injury explains acute pain and persistent neuropathic symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical eruption → **clinical diagnosis**; atypical lesions → vesicle-base VZV PCR
Assess ocular, neurologic, and systemic findings; consider immunodeficiency evaluation for unusually severe/recurrent disease
CSF PCR for suspected CNS infection; do not delay treatment in high-risk presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir** ideally within 72 hours; still treat new lesions or complications
Dissemination, visceral/CNS disease, severe immunosuppression → **IV acyclovir**
Acute pain: acetaminophen/NSAID, add neuropathic agent when needed; avoid routine systemic steroids
Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus glucocorticoid early; eye lubrication/protection for incomplete closure
Postherpetic neuralgia: gabapentin/pregabalin, topical lidocaine, selected TCA; no antiviral benefit after resolved eruption

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent pain >90 days, secondary bacterial infection, corneal injury, vision loss
Meningoencephalitis, vasculopathy, visceral spread in vulnerable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Shingrix two doses** for adults ≥50 years or immunocompromised ≥19 years, including prior zoster
Cover lesions until crusted; exposure causes chickenpox in susceptible contacts, not immediate shingles
Disseminated: airborne/contact until crusted; immunocompromised localized: same precautions until dissemination excluded

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: recurrent localized lesions, often oral/genital rather than a full dermatome
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure pattern, no neuropathic prodrome

human-papillomavirus-infection.name: Human papillomavirus infection
human-papillomavirus-infection.scope: Low-risk HPV and condyloma, high-risk oncogenic HPV (16, 18), anogenital intraepithelial neoplasia and carcinomas, HPV vaccination
human-papillomavirus-infection.core: Most HPV infections clear spontaneously; persistent oncogenic infection causes precancer, while low-risk types cause anogenital warts.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual skin-to-skin contact, new/multiple partners, immunosuppression, HIV
Smoking promotes persistent infection and cervical neoplasia; penetration not required for transmission

rows.label: Clues
items: Condyloma acuminata: painless flesh-colored, verrucous or cauliflower-like genital/perianal growths
High-risk infection usually asymptomatic; postcoital bleeding or abnormal cervical lesion needs diagnostic assessment
★ **Ulceration, induration, fixation, pigmentation, bleeding**, or nonresponse → biopsy rather than empiric retreatment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **HPV 6/11** mainly cause warts; **16/18** account for major oncogenic risk
High-risk E6/E7 interfere with p53/Rb → dysplasia and invasive carcinoma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical external warts → **visual diagnosis**; HPV testing does not guide wart management
Biopsy atypical lesions or uncertain diagnosis, especially with immunosuppression
Cervical HPV/cytology screens for neoplasia; abnormal results → risk-based colposcopy and directed biopsy
No routine HPV screening of asymptomatic partners or blood testing for infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warts: **imiquimod, podofilox, cryotherapy**, or trichloroacetic acid; choose by site, burden, pregnancy
Pregnancy: avoid podofilox/podophyllin; use clinician-applied cryotherapy or acid when treatment needed
High-grade intraepithelial lesions → site-specific ablation/excision; visible suspicious cancer → biopsy and staging
Treatment removes lesions without reliably eradicating virus; asymptomatic infection needs no antiviral

rows.label: Complications
items: Cervical, anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile, and oropharyngeal carcinomas; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
Warts frequently recur; treatment may cause local irritation, ulceration, pigment change

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **9-valent vaccine before exposure**; catch-up through 26 years, shared decision at 27–45 years
AAP: two doses starting <15 years; three if older/immunocompromised; federal 2026 policy differs
Vaccinated people still need cervical screening; condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission

rows.label: Mimics
items: Condyloma lata: broad moist flat secondary-syphilis lesions, positive serology
Molluscum: smooth umbilicated papules; skin tags: soft pedunculated growths

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

macrocytic-anemia.name: Macrocytic anemia
macrocytic-anemia.scope: Folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
macrocytic-anemia.core: MCV >100 fL prompts separation of megaloblastic DNA-synthesis failure from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and marrow disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vegan diet without supplementation, gastric bypass, ileal disease/resection, metformin → B12 depletion
Alcohol misuse, poor intake, pregnancy, methotrexate, trimethoprim → folate depletion
Autoimmune gastritis → pernicious anemia; nitrous oxide functionally inactivates cobalamin

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis; ineffective erythropoiesis may raise LDH/indirect bilirubin and lower other cell lines
★ **Paresthesias, gait ataxia, impaired vibration/proprioception** → B12 deficiency, even without anemia
Smooth macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils indicate megaloblastic change

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective thymidine synthesis delays nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasm
B12-dependent myelin metabolism explains spinal cord/peripheral nerve injury; folate deficiency lacks this syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, smear, reticulocytes, B12**; assess folate, liver tests, TSH, exposures
Borderline B12 → methylmalonic acid; renal impairment can elevate it independently
★ Suspected pernicious anemia → **anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies**; highly specific but not fully sensitive
High reticulocytes → bleeding/hemolysis; unexplained cytopenias/dysplasia → bone marrow evaluation for MDS
Coexisting iron deficiency may normalize MCV; neurologic suspicion still requires B12 evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Replace B12 before or with folate**; folate alone can conceal ongoing neurologic injury
Neurologic/severe deficiency or malabsorption → parenteral B12 initially; irreversible cause requires lifelong replacement
Dietary B12 deficiency may respond to high-dose oral replacement; folate deficiency → oral folic acid
Remove causative drug/exposure where possible; monitor reticulocyte response and count recovery

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated B12 deficiency → irreversible neurologic disability; severe disease → pancytopenia
Pernicious anemia → increased gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumor risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reliable B12 supplementation for vegans**; lifelong monitoring/replacement after relevant GI surgery
Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy; improve nutrition and reduce harmful alcohol intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol-associated macrocytosis: round macrocytes, no required megaloblastic change
Myelodysplasia: persistent multilineage cytopenia, dysplastic marrow
Reticulocytosis: polychromasia after blood loss or hemolysis

macrocytic-anemia.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology and nutritional teaching.

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.name: Medical errors and patient safety
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.scope: Near miss, adverse event, error disclosure, root cause analysis, structured sign-outs and handoffs
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.core: Protect the patient first, disclose errors honestly, and redesign systems to reduce recurrence.

rows.label: Principle
items: Just culture: distinguish human error, risky shortcuts, and reckless conduct
Psychological safety enables reporting; accountability and system improvement can coexist

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Stabilize and mitigate harm**, notify supervising clinician, preserve relevant clinical information
★ Disclose facts, consequences, **apology**, treatment/prevention plans; update uncertainties
★ Report through institutional safety system; document clinical facts and disclosure in medical record

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid concealment, altered records, premature blame, or speculation about causation
Do not rely on education alone when workflow permits predictable repeated errors

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Reckless impairment/dangerous conduct → remove from unsafe duties; institutional escalation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Root cause analysis**: retrospective system investigation; identify multiple contributors
Failure mode and effects analysis: prospective hazard assessment before harm
Handoff: standardized I-PASS/SBAR, pending tasks, contingency plans, receiver synthesis/read-back

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.evidence: Not checked online; established patient-safety terminology and ethical disclosure principles.

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV with relatively preserved hemoglobin and high RBC count suggests thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

nocturnal-enuresis.name: Nocturnal enuresis
nocturnal-enuresis.scope: Primary vs secondary nocturnal enuresis, behavioral modifications, enuresis alarm, desmopressin, secondary etiology workup
nocturnal-enuresis.core: Repeated nighttime wetting after age 5; distinguish isolated developmental bedwetting from new wetting caused by urinary, sleep, metabolic, or psychosocial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, delayed bladder maturation, constipation, sleep-disordered breathing
Secondary episodes may follow stress, diabetes, UTI, or new neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: never dry ≥6 months; secondary: recurrence after ≥6 months dry
Monosymptomatic: no daytime lower urinary symptoms; urgency, weak stream, or daytime leakage changes evaluation
★ Polydipsia, weight loss, continuous dribbling, recurrent UTIs, abnormal gait → **secondary pathology**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nighttime polyuria, reduced functional bladder capacity, and impaired arousal may coexist
Rectal stool burden worsens bladder function; involuntary wetting is not defiance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **History, growth/BP, abdominal/spinal/neurologic examination + urinalysis**; chart voiding, stools, wet nights
Urine glucose for diabetes concern; pyuria/symptoms → urine culture; assess snoring/apnea
Typical primary monosymptomatic disease needs no imaging, urodynamics, or invasive testing
Daytime symptoms, recurrent febrile UTI, continuous leakage, abnormal examination → ultrasound and specialist evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance, regular daytime voiding, bedtime void**, adequate daytime fluids; reduce evening drinks/caffeine
Treat constipation and daytime urinary dysfunction first; reward participation rather than dry nights
★ **Enuresis alarm** for motivated family seeking durable improvement; requires consistent use over weeks
★ **Desmopressin** for rapid short-term control or alarm failure; recurrence common after stopping
Restrict fluids from 1 h before to 8 h after desmopressin; hold during vomiting/diarrhea illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Embarrassment, low self-esteem, avoidance of sleepovers, family conflict
Desmopressin + excess free water → hyponatremia/seizure; imipramine → potentially fatal cardiotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Supportive toileting routines and early constipation treatment; never punish or shame
Periodic treatment breaks assess spontaneous maturation; school/social planning preserves confidence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic ureter: continuous leakage despite normal voids
Diabetes mellitus: polyuria, thirst, glycosuria
UTI: dysuria, frequency, positive culture

nocturnal-enuresis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric continence and desmopressin safety teaching.

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, cognitive decline → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis + alopecia → zinc

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.scope: DEXA scan T-score criteria, screening guidelines, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, bisphosphonates
osteoporosis.core: Fragility fracture or markedly reduced bone density identifies skeletal weakness, often silent until hip or vertebral fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Postmenopause, older age, low BMI, parental hip fracture, smoking, excess alcohol
Glucocorticoids, hypogonadism, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, immobility, rheumatoid arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: Height loss, kyphosis, acute focal back pain after trivial strain suggest vertebral compression
Neurologic deficits, fever, or nocturnal pain suggest alternative spinal pathology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bone resorption exceeds formation; microarchitecture deteriorates despite normally mineralized remaining bone
Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast activity; steroids suppress osteoblasts and reduce calcium balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Hip/spine DXA**; use T-scores in postmenopausal women and men ≥50
★ Hip/vertebral low-trauma fracture establishes diagnosis regardless of DXA; image symptomatic vertebral levels
CBC, calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D; targeted secondary-cause testing
Younger adults: Z-score ≤−2 suggests below-age bone density; T-score alone insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Alendronate or zoledronic acid** for qualifying fracture, osteoporosis-range DXA, or high FRAX risk
Osteopenia: treat if 10-year hip risk ≥3% or major osteoporotic risk ≥20%
Oral bisphosphonate: fasting water, remain upright; avoid esophageal disease, hypocalcemia, severe kidney dysfunction
Very high risk → teriparatide/romosozumab then antiresorptive; stopping denosumab requires follow-on antiresorptive
Vertebral pain: analgesia, mobilization, short bracing; procedures reserved for selected refractory cases

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Hip fracture** → immobility, thromboembolism, excess mortality
Bisphosphonates: rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical femur fracture; denosumab: hypocalcemia, rebound vertebral fractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen **women ≥65**, younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence insufficient for routine male screening
Weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, adequate dietary calcium/vitamin D; minimize tobacco and alcohol
Prednisone-equivalent ≥2.5 mg/day for >3 months → early fracture-risk assessment and preventive treatment by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomalacia: defective mineralization, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Myeloma: anemia, renal injury, lytic lesions; metastatic fracture: destructive focal lesion

osteoporosis.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2025](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening%20); treatment: established fracture-risk framework.

otitis-externa.name: Otitis externa
otitis-externa.scope: Acute diffuse otitis externa, swimmer ear prevention, topical fluoroquinolones, necrotizing otitis externa
otitis-externa.core: Otalgia worsened by moving the pinna or pressing the tragus, with an inflamed external canal, indicates otitis externa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Swimming, moisture, canal trauma from cotton swabs/hearing aids, eczema
Diabetes, older age, immunosuppression → necrotizing infection risk; Pseudomonas often responsible

rows.label: Clues
items: Canal erythema, edema, debris, otorrhea; conductive hearing loss from occlusion
★ **Severe nocturnal pain disproportionate to examination**, granulation tissue → necrotizing otitis externa
Facial weakness or other cranial neuropathy suggests skull-base extension; fever may be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of acidic cerumen barrier permits bacterial proliferation; typical organisms Pseudomonas and S aureus
Necrotizing form invades soft tissue and skull base rather than remaining superficial

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy + tragal/pinna tenderness**; inspect tympanic membrane when visible
Routine uncomplicated cases require no culture or imaging; refractory infection → culture, assess fungal/dermatologic causes
★ Suspected invasive disease → **ESR/CRP, culture, CT temporal bone ± MRI**
Biopsy suspicious persistent granulation to exclude malignancy; MRI better defines soft tissue/cranial involvement

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated → **topical ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin ± steroid**, usually 7–10 days
Gentle canal cleaning; marked edema → wick to deliver drops; acetaminophen/NSAID for pain
Known/suspected perforation or tubes → nonototoxic fluoroquinolone; avoid aminoglycoside/alcohol drops
No routine oral antibiotic unless extension beyond canal, high-risk host, or inability to deliver topical treatment
★ Necrotizing infection → **urgent ENT + systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics**, often prolonged, culture-directed

rows.label: Complications
items: Periauricular cellulitis, canal stenosis, skull-base osteomyelitis, cranial neuropathy
Persistent pain despite drops → reassess technique, obstruction, wrong organism, invasive disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Keep ear dry during treatment; avoid canal instrumentation and cotton swabs
After swimming → dry externally; acidifying drops only with intact membrane and no tubes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute otitis media: middle-ear effusion/bulging TM, little tragal tenderness
Otomycosis: prominent itching, fungal debris, antibiotic-drop history
Mastoiditis: postauricular swelling/tenderness and protruding pinna

otitis-externa.evidence: Not checked online; established otolaryngology topical treatment and invasive-infection principles.

pharyngitis.name: Pharyngitis
pharyngitis.scope: Centor score, Group A Streptococcus, rapid antigen detection, throat culture, viral pharyngitis, penicillin, peritonsillar abscess
pharyngitis.core: Most sore throats are viral; identify patients needing group A streptococcal testing and recognize deep-space infection or airway danger.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: School-age children, close contacts, crowded settings, winter/spring; GAS uncommon below age 3
Smoking, immunosuppression, incomplete vaccination broaden infectious differential

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, oral ulcers** favor viral cause; avoid unnecessary GAS testing
Centor: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough; 1 point each
McIsaac modifies by age; scoring estimates testing need, never proves bacterial infection
★ **Trismus, muffled voice, unilateral bulge, uvular deviation** → peritonsillar abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GAS pharyngeal infection can trigger immune-mediated rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis
Peritonsillar infection progresses into localized pus; deeper spread threatens airway and vessels

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No clear viral syndrome and elevated clinical score → **rapid antigen test or NAAT**
Negative rapid antigen in symptomatic child ≥3 → throat culture; adults usually need no backup
Positive test with compatible illness → treat; asymptomatic carriage generally needs no eradication
Abscess usually clinical; ultrasound/contrast neck CT if uncertain or deep-space extension suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Confirmed GAS → **penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days**; IM benzathine penicillin if adherence uncertain
Penicillin allergy: cephalexin if nonimmediate; azithromycin/clindamycin if immediate, accounting for local resistance
Viral illness → fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen; no antibiotics
★ Peritonsillar abscess → **drainage + amoxicillin-clavulanate**; airway assessment, IV ampicillin-sulbactam if severe

rows.label: Complications
items: Rheumatic fever prevented by timely GAS antibiotics; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis not reliably prevented
Retropharyngeal spread, airway obstruction; Fusobacterium → internal jugular thrombophlebitis/Lemierre syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene; remain home until afebrile and ≥12–24 hours after effective GAS antibiotics
Do not routinely test asymptomatic household contacts or obtain test-of-cure

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV: posterior nodes, splenomegaly, amoxicillin-associated rash
Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod posture, stridor; avoid provocative throat examination
Diphtheria: adherent gray membrane, incomplete vaccination

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.name: Population health and quality improvement
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.scope: Program evaluation, outcome and process measures, health equity, PDSA cycles
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.core: Improve care for a defined population through measurable aims, iterative system changes, and attention to unequal access and outcomes.

rows.label: Principle
items: Population denominator includes eligible people missing visits, not only those receiving care
Equity: stratify outcomes by language, race/ethnicity, geography, disability, insurance, deprivation

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Define **measurable aim**, population, baseline, timeframe; engage patients/frontline staff
★ **PDSA**: plan small change → do → study results → act/adapt before scaling
Stratify measures, address interpreter/transport/cost barriers, monitor unintended consequences

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not assume a favorable outcome proves causation without comparison and context
Avoid blaming individuals for failures created by unreliable workflows

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Run/control charts distinguish routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals over time
Program evaluation: reach, fidelity, effectiveness, cost, sustainability versus original goals

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Process success ≠ patient benefit**; assess both and choose valid denominators
★ **Risk adjustment** improves comparison; also report disparities so adjustment cannot conceal inequity
Before–after improvement may reflect secular trends, case-mix change, regression to mean

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.evidence: Established quality-improvement and program-evaluation principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular activation/CGRP signaling; aura reflects cortical spreading depolarization
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent/disabling migraine → propranolol, topiramate, or CGRP-directed prevention; avoid topiramate/valproate in pregnancy
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

scrotal-masses.name: Scrotal masses
scrotal-masses.scope: Varicocele, hydrocele, spermatocele, testicular cancer differential, physical examination, scrotal Doppler ultrasound
scrotal-masses.core: Painless scrotal swelling requires localization: solid intratesticular lesions are malignant until proven otherwise; many extratesticular lesions are benign.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Testicular cancer: cryptorchidism, prior cancer, family history, younger adult age
Hydrocele: infancy/patent processus vaginalis, trauma, infection; varicocele from venous drainage anatomy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Firm nontransilluminating intratesticular mass** → urgent malignancy assessment
Dull ache/heaviness may occur without acute inflammation; gynecomastia suggests hormone-secreting germ-cell tumor
New isolated right-sided varicocele or failure to decompress supine → evaluate retroperitoneal obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Patent processus vaginalis permits peritoneal-scrotal communication; epididymal duct obstruction forms retention cysts
Pampiniform venous reflux raises local temperature, potentially impairing spermatogenesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Scrotal Doppler ultrasound** localizes intra-/extratesticular lesion and assesses blood flow
Examine standing/supine, with Valsalva; determine whether testis separately palpable and mass transilluminates
Suspected tumor → AFP, beta-hCG, LDH before surgery; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis as needed
Normal markers do not exclude malignancy; AFP elevation excludes pure seminoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspicious testicular mass → **radical inguinal orchiectomy**; avoid transscrotal biopsy
Offer sperm banking before cancer treatment; subsequent surveillance/chemotherapy/radiation depends on histology/stage
Small asymptomatic hydrocele/spermatocele → observe; persistent symptomatic → elective repair
★ Varicocele with **infertility and abnormal semen**, pain, or adolescent testicular atrophy → consider repair

rows.label: Complications
items: Infertility, testicular atrophy; cancer metastasis to retroperitoneal nodes/lungs
Hydrocele may obscure tumor; treatment can impair fertility or endocrine function

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Orchiopexy for undescended testis** reduces infertility risk and facilitates examination; cancer risk persists
No routine population ultrasound or tumor-marker screening; promptly evaluate any new mass

rows.label: Mimics
items: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration
Inguinal hernia: reducible groin-continuous swelling, cough impulse
Epididymitis: tender posterior swelling, urinary/STI findings, increased Doppler flow

secondary-hypertension.name: Secondary hypertension
secondary-hypertension.scope: Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, diagnostic workup
secondary-hypertension.core: Abrupt, unusually young, severe, or resistant hypertension suggests a treatable secondary driver.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, renal disease, adrenal tumors, sleep apnea
NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, stimulants, glucocorticoids, licorice; medication nonadherence can mimic resistance

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypokalemia** suggests mineralocorticoid excess but normal K does not exclude it
Flash pulmonary edema or creatinine rise >30% after ACE inhibitor/ARB → renovascular disease
Endocrine spells, cushingoid appearance, or upper-body hypertension guide cause-specific testing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Renal hypoperfusion activates RAAS; mineralocorticoid signaling increases distal sodium absorption and potassium loss
Catecholamine/cortisol excess, aortic obstruction, or nocturnal hypoxia increases vascular pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **home/ambulatory BP**, adherence, cuff technique; BMP, urinalysis, creatinine, TSH
Sleep-apnea symptoms → polysomnography; abnormal urinary sediment → renal ultrasound and kidney evaluation
★ Biochemical testing precedes adrenal imaging; correct hypokalemia and account for interfering medications
Endocrine Society 2025: suggest **aldosterone screening for all hypertension**, conditional on resources

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Primary aldosteronism: unilateral → **adrenalectomy**; bilateral → spironolactone/eplerenone
Renovascular atherosclerosis → medical risk reduction; revascularize selected recurrent pulmonary edema or refractory disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia → angioplasty; critical bilateral renal stenosis → avoid ACE inhibitor/ARB
★ Pheochromocytoma: **alpha blockade before beta blockade**, volume expansion, then surgery
Treat cortisol source, repair significant coarctation, use CPAP for OSA; stop contributing drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can cause catecholamine crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor renal function/K after RAAS blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists
Genetic evaluation/family screening for suspected hereditary pheochromocytoma or congenital aortic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: normal out-of-office readings
Essential hypertension: gradual course without specific endocrine/renal clues

table.title: Targeted workup
rows: Selective suppression test; CT/adrenal venous sampling
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines

septic-arthritis.name: Septic arthritis
septic-arthritis.scope: Nongonococcal, gonococcal, prosthetic joint infection, IV drug use, empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime), contiguous osteomyelitis
septic-arthritis.core: Acutely painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion → urgent aspiration and drainage; delayed treatment rapidly destroys cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthesis, recent surgery/injection, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteremia
IV drug use → S aureus and gram-negative risk, including Pseudomonas
Young sexually active adults → disseminated gonorrhea; adjacent ulcers/osteomyelitis → contiguous spread

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually acute monoarthritis, often knee; fever may be absent, especially in older/immunocompromised adults
★ **Severe pain with both active and passive motion**; inability to bear weight
Gonococcal dissemination: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules; may progress to purulent monoarthritis
Prosthetic infection: persistent pain, loosening, wound drainage or sinus tract, sometimes minimal systemic illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation → neutrophilic enzymes damage articular cartilage
Implant biofilm limits antibiotic eradication without surgical source control

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Arthrocentesis before antibiotics** when stable: cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Synovial WBC >50,000/µL, neutrophil predominance supports infection; lower counts or negative Gram stain never exclude
★ **Crystals do not exclude infection**; send cultures even when gout seems likely
Blood cultures; gonococcal NAAT from exposed mucosal sites; MRI for suspected contiguous osteomyelitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ After cultures → **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for severe disease, IV drug use, gram-negative risk
Stable low-risk adult: vancomycin ± ceftriaxone based on exposure; narrow to organism/susceptibility
Sepsis → immediate antibiotics without delaying for aspiration; large joints usually need arthroscopic washout
Persistent symptoms → repeat drainage, seek abscess/osteomyelitis; mobilize after infection controlled

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible joint destruction, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, sepsis
Prolonged antibiotics → renal injury, line complications, C difficile; prolonged immobility → stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sterile procedures, treat skin infections, injection-harm reduction
Gonorrhea: treat partners, screen other STIs, abstain until treatment completed and partners treated

rows.label: Mimics
items: Crystal arthritis: polarized crystals; infection still possible concurrently
Bursitis: localized periarticular swelling, passive joint motion relatively preserved
Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory arthritis after GI/GU infection

table.title: Special treatment branches
rows: Debridement, implant retention, prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics

smoking-cessation.name: Smoking cessation
smoking-cessation.scope: Mortality reduction, 5 As counseling, pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement, bupropion, varenicline), behavioral programs
smoking-cessation.core: Stopping tobacco lowers cardiovascular, cancer, pulmonary, and all-cause mortality at any age; counseling plus drugs produces the best quit rates.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **Ask every adult** about tobacco, vaping, dependence, prior attempts; include pregnancy
No readiness to quit → motivational interviewing; connect personal goals to cessation benefits

rows.label: Start/stop
items: 5 As: **Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange**; agree quit date, identify triggers
Arrange early follow-up, behavioral program, quitline; relapse → reassess triggers and renew treatment

rows.label: Test
items: Cigarettes/day, time to first cigarette, withdrawal; no routine biochemical confirmation
Check pregnancy, renal function, seizure/eating-disorder history before selecting drugs

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Nonpregnant adults → **varenicline or combination nicotine replacement** plus behavioral support
Pregnancy → counseling first; if unsuccessful, discuss drugs individually, evidence uncertain

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Psychiatric history alone does not contraindicate varenicline; monitor mood changes
E-cigarettes: insufficient USPSTF evidence for cessation; avoid recommending during pregnancy
Stopping smoke exposure reverses CYP1A2 induction → ↑clozapine/theophylline; nicotine not responsible

table.title: Drug selection
rows: Nausea, vivid dreams; renal dose adjustment
Avoid seizures, eating disorders, abrupt alcohol withdrawal

suicide-risk-assessment.name: Suicide risk assessment
suicide-risk-assessment.scope: Risk and protective factors, lethal means restriction, hospitalization criteria, safety planning
suicide-risk-assessment.core: Assess current suicidal intent, plan, access, past behavior, and ability to remain safe; imminent danger requires immediate protection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior attempt strongest historical predictor; depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, substance use, chronic pain
Recent loss, isolation, incarceration/discharge, agitation, hopelessness, firearm access; older men have high fatality risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Plan + intent + available lethal means**, preparations, or recent attempt → high acute risk
Command hallucinations, intoxication, severe insomnia, impulsivity, inability to collaborate increase concern
Giving away possessions or sudden calm after despair can signal resolved intent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Acute distress, impaired judgment, and accessible lethal methods can convert transient suicidal urges into fatal acts
Protective connections and restricted means increase time and opportunity for intervention

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ask directly** about ideation, intent, plan, timing, access, prior attempts; asking does not induce suicide
Assess depression/mania, psychosis, substance use, violence risk, medical contributors, collateral information
Use structured instruments to support assessment, never as a sole disposition rule
Intoxicated patient → observation and reassessment when clinically sober; initial denial is insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **constant observation, remove hazards, emergency psychiatric evaluation/hospitalization**
Voluntary admission preferred; involuntary protection if serious danger and refusal, following local law
Treat poisoning/injury first; address agitation, withdrawal, mood/psychotic disorder and underlying medical illness
Low acute risk with reliable support → outpatient care only with collaborative plan and rapid follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Fatal or repeated attempts, hypoxic injury, disability, caregiver distress
High vulnerability after emergency/inpatient discharge; abrupt loss of contact raises concern

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safety plan**: warning signs, coping actions, supportive contacts, professional crisis resources, emergency escalation
★ **Lethal means restriction**: secure/remove firearms, limit medication quantities; enlist trusted support
Arrange prompt follow-up and active care linkage; identify reasons for living and dependable supervision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonsuicidal self-injury: no intent to die, but future suicide risk still elevated
Passive death wish: no active plan, still warrants full evaluation
Obsessive intrusive harm thoughts: unwanted/ego-dystonic, without desire or intent to act
